case_analysis.focal_point: Whether oil-and-gas companies can remove Louisiana coastal-damage lawsuits to federal court under the federal-officer removal statute based on their alleged execution of federal directives and contracts—particularly wartime production arrangements—linked to the conduct challenged in the parish complaints.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 28 U.S.C. § 1442(a)(1) (federal-officer removal statute), including the requirement that the defendant was “acting under” a federal officer and that the claims are “for or relating to” acts under color of such office.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (Chevron and other energy companies) argue that removal is proper because (1) they were “acting under” federal officers through federal contractual relationships and federal direction—especially during World War II—where the federal government allegedly enlisted and supervised private industry to secure vital energy supplies; (2) the 2011 amendment expanding removal to claims “for or relating to” acts under color of federal office requires only a connection/association between the challenged conduct and the federally directed activity, not strict causation; (3) they can assert at least one “colorable” federal defense (commonly invoked in § 1442 cases, e.g., derivative sovereign immunity/government-contractor-type defenses or other federal immunities), which is enough at the removal stage; and (4) the Fifth Circuit applied an unduly cramped view of “acting under” and/or the required nexus, effectively allowing state courts to second-guess or burden federally directed operations and undermining § 1442’s purpose of providing a neutral federal forum for disputes implicating federal functions.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents (Plaquemines and Cameron Parishes and Louisiana entities) argue that removal is improper because (1) the parishes’ suits target decades of coastal-wetlands degradation allegedly caused by defendants’ own commercial oil-and-gas exploration, canal dredging, and related activities undertaken for private profit and in alleged violation of state-law duties and permits—not actions carried out under federal officers’ close direction; (2) having federal contracts or operating in a heavily regulated industry (including wartime procurement) does not by itself satisfy “acting under” without the type of subjection, guidance, and control that makes the private party effectively assist the government in carrying out a governmental task; (3) the necessary connection between the plaintiffs’ specific claims and any federally directed conduct is missing—at most defendants point to generalized federal involvement in energy production rather than conduct that the complaints actually challenge; and (4) allowing removal on such attenuated showings would federalize broad swaths of state tort and property litigation whenever defendants can identify some historical federal relationship, contrary to the limited role of § 1442 and the States’ primary authority over their own property and tort law.
key_precedents: Watson v. Philip Morris Cos., 551 U.S. 142 (2007)

John Roberts.reasoning: Petitioners’ strongest point is that Congress’s 2011 addition of “for or relating to” broadened § 1442’s nexus requirement, arguably enough to encompass wartime procurement relationships tied to oil production. But as Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Alito stress, that amendment modifies only the causal-connection prong; it does not displace the distinct, antecedent statutory requirement that the defendant was “acting under” a federal officer in the Watson sense—subjection, guidance, or control while assisting a federal task. On this record, the complaints’ gravamen is decades of profit-driven dredging and canal activity, and petitioners have not tied the specific challenged conduct to contemporaneous federal direction rather than a generalized historical backdrop. Reading “relating to” to supply the missing “acting under” showing would convert a limited federal-officer gateway into a broad industry-based removal entitlement untethered to the statute’s text.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Petitioners’ best point is that Congress’s 2011 insertion of “for or relating to” should be read capaciously enough to capture wartime procurement and federal encouragement of production. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh explain, that amendment concerns only the nexus requirement; it does not displace the antecedent textual prerequisite that defendants were “acting under” a federal officer, which Watson ties to subjection, guidance, or control in aid of a federal task. On this record, the alleged federal involvement looks like a generalized backdrop to an industry, not contemporaneous direction of the particular dredging and coastal-alteration conduct the parishes challenge. Reading “relating to” to do petitioners’ work would effectively convert historical federal demand into a federal-forum entitlement untethered to what defendants were actually directed to do at the time, which the statute’s structure will not bear.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Petitioners’ best point remains that the 2011 addition of “for or relating to” broadened the nexus requirement and could encompass historically significant federal wartime procurement connected to oil production. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh stress, that amendment operates only after the defendant satisfies the statute’s distinct, antecedent condition of “acting under” a federal officer, which Watson demands be shown through subjection, guidance, and control in aid of a federal task—not merely participation in an industry the Government once strongly influenced. Here, as Justice Kagan notes, the operative complaints’ gravamen is decades of defendants’ own profit-driven dredging and extraction decisions, and petitioners have not tethered the specific challenged conduct to contemporaneous federal direction. Reading “relating to” to do the work of “acting under” would distort the statute’s structure and effectively federalize ordinary state-law disputes whenever a defendant can point to generalized, temporally remote federal involvement.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Petitioners’ strongest point is that Congress’s 2011 addition of “for or relating to” was meant to broaden § 1442 removal, and they argue wartime procurement relationships create the requisite connection. But as Justice Kagan and the Chief Justice explain, that amendment speaks to nexus only after the defendant satisfies the distinct threshold requirement of “acting under” a federal officer—Watson’s subjection, guidance, or control in aid of a federal task—and nothing in this record ties federal direction to the particular dredging and canal-building conduct the parishes sue over. Accepting petitioners’ historically inflected theory would invite the very gamesmanship I worry about: defendants could assert thin, temporally remote federal relationships to obtain a federal forum and an appellate “second look,” contrary to Congress’s policy against prolonged jurisdictional litigation. Because the alleged federal involvement is too attenuated from the pleaded wrongs, § 1442 does not authorize removal and remand should stand.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Petitioners’ best point is that Congress’s 2011 amendment broadened § 1442’s nexus requirement to claims “for or relating to” acts under color of office, so wartime procurement might suffice even if not tightly claim-matched. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh stress, that goes only to nexus; it cannot substitute for the antecedent “acting under” requirement, which Watson makes turn on subjection, guidance, or control in aid of a federal task. Looking to the operative complaints, the gravamen is defendants’ own long-running, commercially driven dredging and canal-building decisions allegedly violating state-law duties, with federal wartime relationships at most historically adjacent and not tied to the specific conduct sued upon. Without that federal-officer “anchor,” § 1447(c) makes remand mandatory for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Petitioners’ best shot is the 2011 amendment’s “for or relating to” language, which (they say) allows removal based on a historically looser connection between wartime procurement and later extraction activity. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh stress, that amendment speaks to nexus only after the defendant satisfies the separate statutory gateway of “acting under” a federal officer, which Watson requires to involve subjection, guidance, and control while assisting with a federal task—not merely operating in an industry with past federal demand or regulation. On the pleadings as described, the alleged coastal harms arise from decades of private, profit-driven dredging and canal decisions, and the asserted WWII-era federal relationships appear temporally and factually untethered from the specific conduct being sued upon. Reading “relating to” to do petitioners’ work would effectively collapse the “acting under” requirement and convert § 1442 into a roving federal-forum entitlement, a result the text does not support.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Petitioners’ strongest point remains that the 2011 “for or relating to” amendment loosens the required connection between the claims and federally linked conduct, so WWII procurement relationships should suffice. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Alito stress, that amendment modifies the nexus prong only after the defendant satisfies the distinct, antecedent “acting under” requirement, which Watson demands be shown through subjection, guidance, and control in aid of a federal task—not merely operating in an industry with historic federal demand. On these pleadings, the gravamen is decades of defendants’ own profit-driven dredging and canal-building decisions, and the asserted federal relationships are too generalized and temporally untethered to the specific conduct sued upon. Reading § 1442 to allow removal on that kind of attenuated showing would effectively federalize ordinary state-law property and tort disputes well beyond the statute’s limited purpose.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Petitioners’ strongest point is that Congress’s 2011 addition of “for or relating to” should allow a broader, historically informed nexus between wartime procurement and today’s claims. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh explain, that amendment addresses nexus only after the defendant clears the separate textual gateway of “acting under” a federal officer, which Watson requires to involve subjection, guidance, or control while assisting a federal task—not merely operating in an industry influenced by federal demand. On these pleadings, the challenged dredging and extraction decisions appear long-running and commercially driven, and the asserted federal relationships are too generalized and temporally untethered to the specific acts the parishes sue over. Reading “relating to” to do petitioners’ work would effectively collapse the threshold requirement and turn historical federal involvement into a roving removal entitlement, inconsistent with the statute’s text and our precedents.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Petitioners’ strongest point is that Congress’s 2011 addition of “for or relating to” broadened § 1442’s nexus requirement enough to capture wartime procurement connections, even if indirect. But as Justice Kagan underscores, that amendment cannot do any work unless the defendants first satisfy the distinct, threshold “acting under” requirement that Watson demands—subjection, guidance, or control while assisting a federal task—and the complaints’ gravamen is decades of defendants’ own profit-driven dredging and canal-building choices. Chief Justice Roberts’s emphasis on the mismatch between the pleaded wrongdoing and any contemporaneous federal direction highlights the practical consequence of petitioners’ theory: it would federalize broad swaths of state tort and property litigation based on historically adjacent federal demand, without the procedural-fairness rationale of protecting federally directed conduct. On this record, the asserted federal ties are too generalized and temporally remote to justify federal-officer removal.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1442(a)(1) is textually limited to defendants “acting under” a federal officer, which Watson explains requires subjection, guidance, or control such that the private party is assisting the Government in carrying out a federal task—not merely operating in a regulated industry or selling to the Government. On the face of the parishes’ complaints, the gravamen is decades of privately undertaken canal dredging and oil-and-gas operations allegedly violating state-law duties and permits; the asserted World War II procurement relationships and general federal wartime involvement, as described, do not supply a sufficiently direct link between federal direction and the specific conduct being sued upon. The 2011 “for or relating to” amendment may relax the nexus from strict causation to a genuine connection, but it does not dispense with the threshold “acting under” requirement or authorize removal on an attenuated historical federal relationship untethered to the complained-of acts. Given the forum consequences (remand versus federal adjudication), we should resolve the jurisdictional question now and hold that § 1442 does not reach these state-law coastal-damage suits on this record.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 1442(a)(1) requires, in this statute’s own terms, that the defendant was “acting under” a federal officer and that the state claims are “for or relating to” acts done under color of that office; those phrases demand a concrete, contemporaneous relationship of “subjection, guidance, or control” tied to the specific conduct the complaint challenges, not a historically federalized backdrop for an industry. On the facts described, the parishes sue over decades of canal dredging, wetland damage, and alleged state-law permitting violations undertaken for private production and profit, while petitioners point largely to generalized wartime procurement and federal contracts that do not appear to direct (much less control) the particular dredging and coastal-alteration activities at issue. Reading “relating to” in context cannot be stretched into a categorical safe harbor where any past federal contracting suffices; the required connection must still run to acts performed under federal direction, and nothing suggests these defendants were carrying out a federal officer’s tasks when committing the complained-of environmental harms. Because the asserted federal direction is too attenuated from the pleaded misconduct, removal would improperly expand § 1442 beyond its text and the careful limits recognized in our precedents.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: A close reading of § 1442(a)(1) as a whole confirms that its expanded “for or relating to” language addresses the required nexus, but it does not dilute the distinct threshold requirement that the defendant was “acting under” a federal officer. Under Watson, “acting under” demands more than participation in a regulated industry or ordinary government contracting; it requires subjection, guidance, and control such that the private party is assisting the Government in carrying out a governmental task. On the record described here, the parishes’ complaints target decades of privately driven canal-dredging and extraction activities said to violate state-law duties, and petitioners’ reliance on generalized wartime production arrangements does not supply the necessary link between the specific conduct challenged and any federally directed, supervised performance. Because petitioners have not shown that these suits are “against” them for conduct undertaken while acting under federal direction in the Watson sense, removal is improper and we need not reach broader theories not passed on below.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 1442’s text still requires that defendants be “acting under” a federal officer, and under Watson that means subjection, guidance, and control amounting to assistance in carrying out a federal task—not merely participating in a regulated industry or having historical federal procurement relationships. On these facts, the parishes’ complaints target decades of canal dredging, exploration, and wetlands damage undertaken for defendants’ own commercial ends, and petitioners’ asserted wartime directives and refinery/procurement arrangements are too attenuated from the conduct actually alleged to satisfy the statute’s “for or relating to” nexus even as broadened in 2011. Reading “relating to” to permit removal on such generalized federal involvement would invite strategic invocation of weak federal-officer theories to federalize vast swaths of state tort/property litigation, contrary to Congress’s careful, limited design for federal-officer removal. Because the alleged federal direction does not plausibly map onto the specific challenged acts, and any federal defenses appear speculative at this stage, removal is improper.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Removal under § 1442(a)(1) turns on the case as the parish complaints actually plead it: state-law claims for coastal and wetlands damage allegedly caused by defendants’ own dredging, extraction, and canal-building decisions over decades, undertaken for private profit and allegedly contrary to state duties. Under Watson, being subject to federal regulation or having federal contracts—even wartime procurement arrangements—does not by itself mean the companies were “acting under” a federal officer; the defendant must be assisting the Government in carrying out a federal task under close direction and control, and the suit must be for or relating to those directed acts. On this record, the asserted WWII refining/production relationships are at most historically adjacent to the challenged conduct and do not supply the claim-specific connection that § 1442 requires, so the federal-officer “anchor” for removal is missing and the case belongs in state court.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 1442(a)(1) requires that the defendant be “acting under” a federal officer and that the suit be “for or relating to” acts under color of that office, and Watson teaches that ordinary regulation or participation in a regulated industry—even an important one—does not suffice without subjection, guidance, and control amounting to assistance in carrying out a federal task. On these pleadings, the parishes’ claims target defendants’ long-running, profit-driven canal-dredging and extraction activities alleged to violate state-law duties and permits; the asserted World War II procurement relationships and generalized federal encouragement of oil production are too attenuated from the specific conduct the complaints challenge to satisfy even the broadened “relating to” nexus. Because the threshold “acting under” and case-linked “relating to” requirements are not met on the present record, the statute’s text does not authorize removal, leaving Louisiana courts to adjudicate these state tort and property claims. That conclusion follows from treating § 1442 as a jurisdictional gateway whose terms must be satisfied as written, without converting any historical federal involvement in energy production into a roving license to federalize state-law litigation.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 1442 removal requires that the defendant was “acting under” a federal officer—meaning the kind of subjection, guidance, and control that makes the private party assist the Government in carrying out a federal task—not merely operating in a regulated industry or supplying a product the Government wants. On these facts, the parishes’ complaints target decades of privately profit-driven canal dredging, exploration, and coastal-wetlands damage, and petitioners have not shown that federal wartime procurement arrangements specifically directed, controlled, or required the particular dredging/operations the complaints challenge. The 2011 “for or relating to” language may loosen the nexus requirement, but it does not eliminate the antecedent “acting under” requirement or permit removal based on an attenuated historical federal relationship untethered to the pleaded misconduct. Allowing removal on these generalized showings would expand § 1442 beyond its separation-of-powers purpose of protecting federally directed functions and would federalize ordinary state tort/property disputes without the necessary federal-officer relationship.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The threshold question is statutory coverage: whether these oil-and-gas companies were “acting under” a federal officer with respect to the conduct the parishes actually challenge—decades of canal dredging, extraction, and wetlands damage tied to defendants’ commercial operations. Under Watson, a regulated or contracting relationship is not enough; removal requires the kind of subjection, guidance, and control that makes the private party assist the Government in carrying out a governmental task, and the record as described links federal direction chiefly to wartime procurement/production arrangements rather than to the specific coastal-damage activities alleged in the complaints. The 2011 addition of “or relating to” relaxes the nexus inquiry once “acting under” is satisfied, but it does not eliminate the need for a concrete connection between the claims and federally directed acts; on these facts, the asserted federal involvement is too generalized and temporally attenuated to convert state-law coastal tort/property suits into § 1442 cases. Because § 1442 serves important federal-forum interests, it should be applied where federal direction is genuinely implicated—but not stretched to federalize broad swaths of state litigation based on historical federal relationships untethered to the pleaded wrongs.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Applying § 1442(a)(1) as construed in Watson, petitioners have not shown they were “acting under” a federal officer with the kind of subjection, guidance, and direct control that transforms private commercial extraction and canal-dredging into assistance in carrying out a federal duty. Even accepting wartime procurement and contracting as historically significant, the parish complaints target decades of coastal-wetlands damage arising from defendants’ own operational choices and alleged state-law permit and property violations, not conduct plausibly undertaken at the federal government’s direction in the challenged locations and time periods. The 2011 “for or relating to” language relaxes nexus compared to strict causation, but procedural fairness and practical consequences counsel against allowing removal on a generalized, attenuated association that would federalize large swaths of state tort/property litigation whenever an industry can point to past federal contracts. Because the asserted federal relationship is too remote from the specific alleged wrongdoing, a neutral federal forum is not warranted on this record.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether oil companies that produced fuel under federal contracts and wartime direction during World War II may remove Louisiana coastal-damage suits to federal court under the federal-officer removal statute by showing they were “acting under” federal officers and have a colorable federal defense connected to the complained-of conduct.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (Chevron and others) argue that removal is proper because, during WWII, they performed critical wartime fuel production and supply functions under federal direction through contracts and intensive supervision that made them private parties “acting under” federal officers. They contend the statute is meant to be interpreted broadly to protect federal operations from state-court interference and that the Fifth Circuit applied an unduly cramped test for “acting under” and/or the required nexus (“for or relating to” the acts under color of federal office). Petitioners also maintain they have at least a colorable federal defense (e.g., defenses tied to federal direction/authority and federal interests in wartime procurement), which is all § 1442 requires at the removal stage, and that the parishes’ claims—though styled as state tort/coastal restoration claims—relate to activities undertaken to carry out federal wartime objectives.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents (Plaquemines Parish, Cameron Parish, and Louisiana entities) argue removal is improper because the parishes’ suits target long-running extraction, canal dredging, and wetlands damage in Louisiana, not conduct performed under federal officers in a manner that satisfies § 1442. In their view, the companies were ordinary commercial actors that sold products to the government and were subject to regulation or contracting terms, which is insufficient under Supreme Court precedent to qualify as “acting under” a federal officer. They also argue petitioners cannot establish the necessary causal/nexus requirement because the complained-of coastal damage is not “for or relating to” any specific federally directed wartime acts, and petitioners’ asserted federal defenses are not sufficiently tied to the parishes’ claims. Respondents and supporting amici further frame the litigation as a core state-law matter involving local land loss and remediation responsibilities that should remain in state court absent a clear and direct federal-officer relationship to the alleged misconduct.
key_precedents: Watson v. Philip Morris Cos., 551 U.S. 142 (2007)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch is right that the 2011 amendment’s “for or relating to” language broadens the nexus inquiry and that § 1442 operates as a threshold gateway rather than a merits trial. But that textual expansion does not displace Watson’s independent “acting under” requirement—subjection, guidance, or control in assisting a federal superior with a federal task—and, as Justice Barrett underscores, petitioners’ showing is too generalized to tie the parishes’ specific dredging/extraction conduct to any identified federally directed work. Reading “relating to” to do all the work here would be an oblique and consequential expansion of federal jurisdiction, effectively converting ordinary procurement relationships into a broad removal right without clear congressional authorization. On this record, the presumption against such sweeping jurisdictional displacement is not overcome, though a more particularized showing in another case could satisfy § 1442.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch is correct that § 1442 is a threshold gateway and that Congress broadened the nexus in 2011 to include suits “for or relating to” acts under color of office. But that broader nexus does not dispense with Watson’s distinct “acting under” requirement, which demands more than generic assertions about wartime procurement; it requires a concrete showing of “subjection, guidance, or control” over the particular conduct the plaintiffs challenge. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, petitioners have not tied the parishes’ specific dredging/extraction and coastal-loss mechanisms to identified federally directed tasks, so the asserted federal defenses remain untethered from the pleaded misconduct. Treating background federal purchasing as sufficient would collapse the jurisdictional gatekeeping function of § 1442 and effectively convert it into a general contractor-removal provision without textual warrant.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch is right to stress that Congress broadened the nexus requirement in 2011 to include suits “for or relating to” acts under color of office, and that §1442 removal is a threshold inquiry. But that amendment did not alter the statute’s separate requirement that the defendant was “acting under” a federal officer in the Watson sense—meaning subjection, guidance, or control in carrying out a federal task—and petitioners’ showing remains at too high a level of generality to connect the parishes’ specific dredging/extraction and wetlands-loss allegations to any identified federal directive. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, accepting wartime procurement in the background as sufficient would effectively transform §1442 into a broad contractor-removal provision untethered from the text Congress enacted. Because the asserted federal defenses are not concretely linked to the particular conduct the complaints challenge, the jurisdictional predicates for removal are not satisfied on this record.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch is right that § 1442 is meant to be a threshold gateway and that Congress’s 2011 addition of “or relating to” broadened the nexus inquiry, so removal should not demand a merits trial. But even at the threshold, the statute’s separate “acting under” requirement—Watson’s demand for subjection, guidance, or control in assisting federal officers with a federal task—must have real content, and on this record the proffer is still too generalized and untethered to the complained-of dredging/extraction conduct. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, letting wartime procurement in the background do all the jurisdictional work would predictably incentivize thin federal-officer theories to secure a federal forum and prolong jurisdictional fights Congress sought to avoid. A broader “relating to” cannot erase the need for a concrete, claim-linked showing that the challenged acts were performed under federal direction, so I would affirm remand.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch is correct that Congress broadened § 1442’s nexus in 2011 to “for or relating to,” and that removal is a threshold inquiry not a merits trial. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, that amendment does not alter the statute’s separate prerequisite that the defendant was “acting under” a federal officer in the Watson sense—assisting with a federal task subject to federal guidance or control over the relevant conduct—and petitioners’ showing remains too generalized to connect the parishes’ dredging/extraction allegations to any identified federally directed work. If the proffered wartime procurement relationship sufficed without a claim-linked showing, § 1442 would become a broad contractor-removal device untethered to the pleaded conduct, contrary to Congress’s limited jurisdictional grant. Given our continuous duty to ensure subject-matter jurisdiction, the absence of an adequate statutory hook requires remand on this record.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Chief Justice and Justice Barrett press the strongest objection: that petitioners’ showing is too generalized and risks turning § 1442 into a broad “procurement contractor” removal device. But § 1442(a)(1) asks whether defendants plausibly were “acting under” a federal officer and whether the suit is “for or relating to” acts under color of that office; Congress in 2011 adopted expansive connective text (“relating to”) and did not require a claim-by-claim, site-specific evidentiary demonstration at the removal gateway. Watson surely demands more than mere regulation or ordinary commerce, yet wartime production undertaken to meet federal needs pursuant to federal direction can qualify as “acting under,” with disputes about which precise dredging or extraction choices were federally specified left for merits or jurisdictional factfinding in federal court. I am reluctant to graft onto the statute an atextual heightened-linkage requirement—especially one that risks collapsing the procedural removal inquiry into a mini-trial about the parishes’ particularized allegations.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch is right that § 1442 is a threshold gateway and that the 2011 addition of “or relating to” broadens the nexus inquiry, so courts should not demand that the federal defense be proven on the merits at removal. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, that amendment does not dilute Watson’s independent “acting under” requirement, which still demands a concrete, claim-linked showing of subjection, guidance, or control over the particular conduct alleged. On this record, petitioners’ proffer remains at too high a level of generality—wartime procurement in the background without specific linkage to the decades of Louisiana extraction/dredging and canal work the parishes target—so the asserted federal defenses are not meaningfully connected to the charged acts for § 1442 jurisdiction. Treating such attenuated historical association as sufficient would effectively transform federal-officer removal into a broad contractor-removal statute, which the text does not support.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch is right that the 2011 addition of “or relating to” broadens § 1442’s nexus inquiry and that removal is a threshold determination, not a merits trial. But as the Chief Justice emphasizes, that amendment did not alter Watson’s independent “acting under” requirement, which demands a concrete showing of subjection, guidance, or control in assisting a federal superior with respect to the conduct the complaint targets. Here the proffered wartime procurement relationship remains too generalized to link the parishes’ specific dredging/extraction-and-coastal-damage allegations to federally directed acts, and “relating to” cannot do the work of collapsing that threshold statutory predicate. On this record, affirming remand is the straightforward application of Watson and our insistence that consequential jurisdictional displacement rest on a clear statutory fit.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s strongest point is that §1442 is a threshold gateway and that the 2011 “or relating to” amendment loosens the nexus inquiry, so we should not demand a merits-level showing at removal. But even at the threshold, the removing party bears the burden to establish the statute’s jurisdictional predicates with something more concrete than intuition about wartime procurement; “relating to” cannot collapse Watson’s separate “acting under” requirement into mere historical association. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, petitioners have not identified evidence of federal “subjection, guidance, or control” over the specific extraction/dredging practices the parishes challenge, and without that claim-linked showing the asserted federal defenses are too untethered to support removal. Treating generalized WWII contracting as sufficient would effectively expand §1442 beyond its limited jurisdictional grant and do so in a way that is inconsistent with evenhanded, disciplined application of Article III’s gatekeeping norms.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1442(a)(1) requires that the defendant was “acting under” a federal officer and that the suit is “for or relating to” acts done under color of federal office; reading those words in their ordinary sense and in light of the statute’s jurisdictional role, we do not infer a sweeping displacement of the usual state-court forum absent a concrete showing tied to the claims at issue. Under Watson, supplying goods to the Government—even under wartime contracts and regulation—does not by itself establish “acting under” unless the companies were assisting federal officers in carrying out governmental duties through subjection, guidance, or control over the relevant work. Here, the parishes’ complaints target decades-long extraction, canal dredging, and wetlands degradation in Louisiana, and petitioners have not shown that the particular conduct alleged was undertaken pursuant to direct and detailed federal direction such that the claims are “for or relating to” those federally supervised acts. Given that mismatch, petitioners’ asserted federal defenses are not sufficiently connected to the complained-of conduct to justify the consequential shift of these state-law suits into federal court on an oblique jurisdictional theory.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 1442 requires more than generic assertions that defendants once supplied the Federal Government during wartime; it demands a specific, pleaded connection between the parishes’ complained-of conduct—Louisiana extraction practices, canal dredging, and resulting wetlands loss—and acts the companies performed “under” a federal officer’s direction. Under Watson, ordinary contracting and regulation are insufficient absent a showing of subjection, guidance, or control in the particular operations that allegedly caused the coastal damage, and the record as described relies too heavily on broad wartime production efforts rather than federally directed conduct tied to the alleged dredging and land-loss mechanisms. The “for or relating to” nexus likewise is not satisfied by pointing to incidental federal procurement activity in the background; the removing defendants must link the parishes’ specific tort theories to federally supervised tasks, not to generalized “decisionmaking” or overall fuel production. Because petitioners have not shown that the alleged coastal-harm conduct itself was carried out to assist federal officers in a way that supplies the necessary nexus, they cannot establish a colorable federal defense connected to the claims sufficient to justify federal-officer removal here.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 1442(a)(1) demands a provision-specific showing that defendants were “acting under” a federal officer and that the suit is “for or relating to” acts taken under color of that office; it is not enough to invoke wartime contracting in the abstract. Under Watson, private parties qualify only when they are assisting federal officers in carrying out governmental tasks under a relationship of subjection, guidance, or control, and the record as framed here ties the parishes’ alleged injuries—decades of canal dredging, extraction, and coastal degradation in Louisiana—to long-running commercial operations rather than to discrete, federally directed WWII production tasks. Even accepting that wartime fuel production involved contracts and supervision, petitioners have not connected the specific conduct complained of in these coastal-damage suits to any particular federal directive in a way that satisfies the “for or relating to” nexus or makes their asserted federal defenses colorably applicable to the alleged wetlands harms. Because the lower-court analysis must be anchored to the operative statutory requirements and the concrete allegations, removal fails on this record.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 1442 is textually limited to defendants “acting under” a federal officer, which Watson explains requires more than ordinary commercial contracting or regulation—there must be subjection, guidance, or control such that the private party is assisting the Government in carrying out a federal task. Even accepting that wartime fuel procurement involved significant federal direction, the parishes’ complaints target decades of Louisiana extraction practices, canal dredging, and coastal-wetlands damage, and petitioners have not tied that challenged conduct “for or relating to” federal direction with the kind of specific, work-linked control Watson demands. Reading § 1442 broadly enough to cover any company that once supplied the Government would invite strategic removals on attenuated federal-contract theories, undermining Congress’s calibrated allocation of jurisdiction and encouraging the very prolonged jurisdictional fights our precedents warn against. Because petitioners have not shown the necessary “acting under” relationship and a concrete connection between federally directed acts and the alleged coastal harms, removal is improper.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1442 is a jurisdictional grant, and the removing defendants must satisfy its text by showing they were “acting under” a federal officer and that the suit is “for or relating to” acts taken under color of that office. On this record, the parishes’ complaints target decades of Louisiana extraction, canal dredging, and coastal-wetlands damage—conduct that looks like ordinary commercial operations—while the asserted World War II procurement relationship chiefly shows the companies sold fuel to the Government, not that they were delegated a federal task and subjected to the kind of “subjection, guidance, or control” that Watson demands. Even assuming some wartime contracts involved close supervision, petitioners have not tied the complained-of coastal damage to those federally directed acts in a way that satisfies § 1442’s nexus requirement as applied to these pleadings; the federal interest in wartime supply is too attenuated from the specific injuries alleged. Because Congress has not authorized removal on a broader theory than § 1442’s requirements, and those requirements are not met here, jurisdiction is lacking and remand follows.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 1442(a)(1) asks whether the defendants were “acting under” a federal officer, whether the suit is “for or relating to” acts under color of federal office, and whether a “colorable” federal defense is asserted—and the text sets a procedural gateway, not a merits trial. On these pleadings and removal proffer, wartime fuel production and supply pursuant to federal contracts and intensive federal direction is plausibly more than mere compliance with regulation or an ordinary arms-length sale; it is assistance in carrying out a federal function, satisfying “acting under” as Watson framed it. Congress’s 2011 addition of “or relating to” broadens the required connection, so Louisiana’s coastal-damage claims need only bear an association to the federally directed wartime production activities, not be caused exclusively by a single identified federal command, and any disputes about the scope of direction go to the merits later. Because petitioners assert at least a colorable federal defense tied to wartime federal authority and procurement direction, the statute’s text entitles them to a federal forum without importing extra-textual, heightened nexus requirements.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 1442 requires more than ordinary commercial contracting or regulatory compliance; the removing defendant must show it was “acting under” a federal officer by assisting the Government in carrying out federal duties with subjection, guidance, or control, and must connect the suit’s “charged conduct” to those federally directed acts. On this record, the parishes’ claims target decades of Louisiana extraction practices, canal dredging, and resulting wetlands loss, and petitioners have not shown with sufficient specificity that the complained-of coastal-damage conduct was performed pursuant to wartime federal direction rather than general private operations that happened to include supplying fuel to the Government. Nor have petitioners adequately tied a colorable federal defense to the particular alleged misconduct that caused the asserted injuries, as opposed to invoking WWII procurement and supervision at a high level of generality. Given the statute’s threshold jurisdictional character and the need for a concrete, evidence-grounded connection between federal direction and the specific acts alleged, removal is not warranted here.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 1442(a)(1)’s text requires that the defendant be “acting under” a federal officer, which Watson construes to mean assisting or helping carry out a federal superior’s duties—something that goes beyond ordinary commercial activity, even when heavily regulated or performed under standard procurement contracts. On the facts presented, petitioners’ showing looks too generalized: producing and selling fuel during WWII under federal contracts and wartime directives does not, without evidence of unusually close, direct, and detailed federal control over the specific extraction/dredging/canal practices alleged to have caused Louisiana’s coastal damage, establish the requisite “subjection, guidance, or control.” The statute’s “for or relating to” language is broader than the old causal-nexus test, but it still demands a concrete connection between the federally directed conduct and the complained-of acts; here the parishes’ claims target decades of local operational decisions not tied to any identified federally commanded wartime acts. And while §1442 demands only a colorable federal defense at the threshold, that defense must be connected to the conduct at issue; petitioners have not shown, with the necessary specificity, that the asserted federal wartime direction plausibly governs liability for the particular coastal harms alleged.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Petitioners, as the parties invoking federal jurisdiction through § 1442(a)(1) removal, bear the burden to establish with evidence (not intuition or broad wartime rhetoric) that they were "acting under" a federal officer and that the parishes’ coastal-damage claims are "for or relating to" the specific federally directed conduct. On this record, the asserted link appears to depend on layered, third-party and time-extended causal chains—i.e., that federal wartime procurement decisions dictated the particular extraction, canal dredging, and wetlands-altering activities Louisiana challenges—yet petitioners have not adduced concrete facts showing federal “subjection, guidance, or control” over the complained-of conduct as opposed to ordinary commercial production and sale. Watson makes clear that heavy regulation or contracting, without a showing of assisting federal officers in carrying out governmental tasks through direct and detailed control, is insufficient; and the 2011 “relating to” language cannot be used to erase that threshold requirement. Because petitioners have not carried their evidentiary burden to demonstrate the necessary federal-officer relationship and claim-connection for removal, I would affirm remand to state court.
